utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. No preliminaries. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Glogovac. Before you give evidence, the Rules require you to make a solemn declaration. May I invite you to make that declaration, of which the text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You'll find him to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good morning.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to speak your name as slowly as possible for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: My name is Radovan Glogovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Glogovac, at any point in time did you provide a statement to the Defence of General Mladic, a written statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please look at document 1D01687 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Glogovac, this is the first time you're appearing before this Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We will go more slowly. Could you please look at the screen in front of you and there you see your statement. And my question will be: Is this your information, are these your particulars, and is that your signature on this page?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, it is my signature and the data is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at the last page of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Glogovac, is this your signature on this page and is the date that is written there written by your hand?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, the signature and the date are in my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we were preparing for you to appear before the Tribunal today, did you point out three errors in the information in this statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave I would just like us to look at paragraph 1 of the statement, line 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where it states: "At the faculty of economics in Subotica ..." Does it not -- is what is omitted here that "studied" -- the word "studied at the faculty of economics in Subotica"?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at paragraph 21 of the statement, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 21, line 2, you indicated the following words: "Dr. Stamenkovic was killed in Zepca." Should the person's last name be different?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, it should be Dr. Vaskovic, Dr. Djordje Vaskovic. It was my error.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the transcript I see line 17, page 3, where it says -- ah, it's been corrected. All right. Thank you so much. Dr. Djordje Vaskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In lines 5 and 6 of paragraph 21 of the statement in the B/C/S version, there is the words: "Fire was opened on a vehicle of a Serb, Obrenovic, a Heckler weapon," and then it says: "That was when Milojevic was wounded." Could you please tell us whether the last name of this person is Milovic or Milojevic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: His last name was Milovic. Actually I'm related to him on my mother's side and I knew him quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now today when you made these three corrections in your statement, if I -- after you made the corrections, now, if I were to put the same questions to you that I put to you in the statement, would your answers be identical to the ones you gave in your written statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, except there is a mistake. I had said that the number of Serbs in Zenica was 27.000 but actually the exact number is 22.433. That's the exact number. It was an error during some talks that we had, so we -- we included others who did not declare themselves as Serbs, about 5.000 of them, so this is what the error was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we now please look at paragraph 5 of the witness statement. Paragraph 6. Paragraph 6 of the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Glogovac, you said here that about 27.000 Serbs lived there before the war. Today you're making a correction and you're saying that the number is -- could you please repeat it for the transcript?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: The official information according to the consensus was 22.433 Serbs. This is the actual figure. When I was dealing with those figures in negotiations, we included about 15.000 Yugoslavs all together, so we split that figure giving 5.000 to Serbs, 5.000 to Croats, and 5.000 to Muslims, and this is what this mistake is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that you have clarified this, I'm putting the question to you again: Taking into account the three corrections, today, after you have given the solemn declaration, would you stand by the answers that you provided in your written statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender the witness statement of Witness Radovan Glogovac, and that would be number 1D01687.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President. I don't object in this case. But just to lay down a marker, corrections like that, that are made beforehand, we would normally expect to receive some notice of and I haven't in this instance. In this case we don't consider ourselves prejudiced and so we don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1687 receives number D619, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honours, I would like to read the summary of Mr. Radovan Glogovac's statement now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Witness Radovan Glogovac, together with his family, in 1992 lived and worked in Zenica where he was also politically engaged in duties of the vice-president of the local SDS party. He took part in numerous negotiations between the political leadership of the Muslims, Serbs, and Croats with the objective of calming political and interethnic tensions in that area already after the war broke out in Croatia. He will testify about the attitude towards Serb cadres in the municipality, about deterioration of interethnic relations, and the Serbs escaping from this region. Some left on their own; others were expelled, arrested, and held captured in the correctional facility of Zenica, some 4- to 500 of them, or some were killed. He will speak about the blockades and attacks on JNA barracks, about pulling out the men and equipment from Zenica, and about the departure of the Serb civilian population from this area after the JNA left Zenica on the 18th of May 1992. During that time-period several attacks on Serb villages occurred starting from the 11th of May 1992. There was an attack on the village of Svice. There were a number of killings of Serbs in the Zenica area. The Mujahedin came to these areas which caused even more insecurity among the Serb population. After leaving Zenica on the 7th of June 1992, he got a job at the government of Republika Srpska as an associate, and he worked on population exchanges as member of the commission for the exchange of persons in the territory of central Bosnia. He participated in several negotiations with the opposing sides about organising exchanges, and is a direct participant of a number of implemented exchanges. He will talk specifically about his role and the assignments which he was given from Minister Ostojic in the process of bringing out the Croatian population over Mount Vlasic towards Croatia. They were instructed to receive the population and take care of them in a professional manner. He was in contact with the local commander, Janko Trivic, about the implementation of this assignment, and he had the opportunity to see a dispatch by the VRS Main Staff on the arrival of Croats from Central Bosnia. HVO soldiers that came to RS territory with the civilian population handed over their weapons, and when they left the area the weapons were returned to them and the civilian population continued on their way towards Gradiska and Okucani. This is a short summary of the witness's statement. And by your leave, Your Honours, I would just like to put a few questions to the witness now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed as you suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at paragraph 7 of the statement, which now has the number -- actually, I didn't manage to write down the exact -- the correct number, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: D -- it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- for the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is D619.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D619. Thank you very much, Your Honour. So let's look at D619, paragraph 7, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Glogovac, when you described your role in these difficult times - we're talking about paragraph 7 now - you spoke about specific assignments that you had in negotiations with the Muslim side. Since you were the vice-president of the SDS, how did it come about for you to find yourself in the middle of all of these negotiations about the exchanges?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: During the elections in the Serbian Democratic Party in Zenica, Dr. Slobodanka Hrvacanin was elected president, and I was elected vice-president. As the tensions grew in Zenica, we were informed that they were preparing to liquidate her. The information came from very high-up figures in the police. They said that she could not be protected. She left Zenica and went to Banja Luka with her family. I confirm this. And then after she tried to move her things out from her flat in Zenica, a truck came and then there was a conflict between our workers that we had sent to load her things and some local strongmen. This was one of the first interethnic conflicts, actually. You could say that. So she had to leave Zenica because we could not provide security for her. According to the statute, I took over all of her duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at paragraph 13 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is your statement, D619. This is where you say that the Muslim authorities did not allow the Serbs to leave Zenica. So I am asking you why did the authorities in Zenica act in this way?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the first reason was because they wanted to present the situation in Zenica as being a multiethnic one. Even though a lot of Serbs had left Zenica, they put up blockades on the road from Zenica towards Doboj so that buses were not able to leave. I thought about what the second reason could be, and that was that we were some sort of human shields. So the propaganda in Zenica was such that they were saying that Serbs were expected to enter the town of Zenica from all sides and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at paragraphs 20 -- paragraph 25 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: There you describe negotiations on one occasion with the authorities in Zenica, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and you talk about how they offered you that you should surrender the area of Zenica to the VRS so that armed hostilities would cease. Could you please tell the Court what happened? How did this come about?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: There was a meeting in Turbe, near Travnik, and to my surprise, for the first time we managed to speak with the representatives from Zenica in a normal way. We managed to exchange a number of civilians, arrange humanitarian aid, and that was where they presented to me an old-fashioned instrument, gusla, and that made me feel that they appreciated my work. After searching my apartment, they brought that from my apartment and they gave me that musical instrument. They allowed 1500 Serbs to leave Zenica. So --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please slow down. Perhaps you resume. You said: "After searching my apartment, they brought that from my apartment and they gave me that musical instrument." Could you resume from there? You said, "They allowed ..." and then continue from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, but I don't have much experience in testifying like this. I will try to speak as slowly as possible. So they did give me the instrument. They allowed people to leave. They decided to permit 1500 Serbs from leaving Zenica. They proposed that the part that they were controlling, that they would lay down their weapons in that area, that there would be no war. They didn't mean that forces of Republika Srpska should enter that part and control Zenica. They just meant that there would be a suspension of combat and that we could arrange through the bar port to ship large quantities of aid from the United States which would meet everybody's needs. So I was really very satisfied. And there was a Professor Dokic who was also participating in the negotiations, replied from our side that we gladly accept that. And if they were able to guarantee that there would be no fighting and that the extremist groups in that area, the Mujahedin and so on, would surrender their weapons, and that this whole area would become a peaceful area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would appreciate it if you would answer briefly. I see your answer to this next question in this paragraph, but what, according to you, is the reason why the Muslims changed their position in December 1993?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: They had fierce clashes with Croats in western Bosnia at that time. They claimed they were receiving aid through Luka and Ploce, et cetera, and they claim that the Croats skimmed 50 per cent off that because those were Croat ports. And that's why they wanted to restore some peace with the Serbs, not to wage war anymore. I asked them how they meant to do this in view of their government in Sarajevo. They said, "We don't care. We just don't want to be at war anymore."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we look at paragraph 36 of your statement, please. In this paragraph you described your participation in the process of dislocating the Croat civilians and military. Could you just tell the Court, very briefly, what your role and tasks were in this process?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: At that time I was working at the office of Minister Velibor Ostojic, who was then a minister without portfolio, and deputy vice -- deputy prime minister, and he told me to urgently report to military authorities in Banja Luka and in Vlasic to see how they would receive a large number of Croat refugees in the area of Vlasic and partly in Donji Vakuf and via Kupres. My task was to report on a daily basis what is needed - fuel, buses, et cetera. I went to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps and they told me to go see the commander at Mount Vlasic. I believe it was the 22nd Brigade. I had to see Lieutenant-Colonel Janko Trivic, whom I didn't know. Trivic received me, showed me an order of the Main Staff, and I saw that the orders were made to supply [Realtime transcript ready in error "shares"] chairs for Croat officers, everything according to Geneva Conventions. I was present several times when groups departed. Buses were waiting for civilians to take them to Gradiska, to Novska. The able-bodied military-aged men were, of course, routed differently and taken away in different directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, as representative of the civilian authorities of Republika Srpska, or Mr. Trivic as the representative of military authorities, at any point have any instructions for unlawful treatment of this population? Did you have instructions to hinder their passage through Republika Srpska or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: No. Emphatically no. Neither Mr. Trivic nor I had any such instructions. On the contrary, with all the problems that I had to deal with, I had to report to the Deputy Prime Minister, Velibor Ostojic, if anything was not going well. I had instructions that if I encountered any problems, I had to report to Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would only like to tender one accompanying exhibit, 1D03712, one associated exhibit. And that would be the conclusion of my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Any objections? No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D3712 receives number D620, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Before I invite the Prosecution to cross-examine the witness, I would have two questions. You said you saw orders. "The orders were made to supply shares for Croat officers." What did you mean exactly with "to supply shares"? Was it chairs? Yes. Yes, then perhaps it -- on the transcript we read "shares," but "supplying chairs in line with the Geneva Conventions," is that -- I was just wondering what exactly you meant by that or to what extent that is covered by any legal instrument.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, that's not exactly what I said. I said I had seen the order of General Mladic on how to receive the refugees from Central Bosnia, and I wanted to clarify that I saw Mr. Trivic, the commander, take all the measures to make sure that everything was in keeping with Geneva Conventions. And before me, he gave orders to his subordinate officers on how to receive Croat officers, to provide them with so many chairs and so much furniture in the rooms where they would be accommodated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now does --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not what the statement says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the statement, then. I was looking at the transcript, as a matter of fact, but ... Well, the statement in this respect leaves it open whether specifically the chairs were mentioned in the order or whether the order just said that they should be received in the humane and professional manner. I have no -- I don't want to further explore this. There was another matter which I would like to ask you about, which is the following: You said -- one second, please. You said you were present several times when groups departed. You're talking about buses waiting for civilians and where they were taken. And then you said: "The able-bodied military-aged men were, of course, routed differently and taken away in different directions." Could you tell me why, of course, able-bodied military-aged men were routed differently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as far as I know there was an agreement with the Croatian side. And when we were negotiating about those people with whom there were no problems, civilians, et cetera, they could immediately depart via Gradiska and Novska, whereas the others, as agreed with the Croatian side, would be allowed to depart after we ran certain checks because we had information that there were among them war criminals. Especially in the area of Jajce there had been heinous war crimes. And after these checks, they were allowed to depart after only a brief delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you find any war criminals during those checks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, we did not and nobody was kept. Nobody was held back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Traldi. You'll find Mr. Traldi to your right. Mr. Traldi is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Traldi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And to pick up where the Presiding Judge just left off, do you know where those checks for war criminals were conducted?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I cannot say with any certainty at which location, but as far as I know -- I mean, I don't really know where the checks were carried out. I know that some military-aged men were kept at Manjaca for a short time and after that they were sent off to the so-called Herceg Bosna as it was known at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll leave that topic now and I want to turn back to 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, I nevertheless would have one question. If you said they were kept at Manjaca for a short time, what do you mean by "a short time"? One or two days, one or two weeks, or one or two months, or six months? What is "a short time" for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up to six days. That's what I mean by "short time."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how do you know that, that they were released after six days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I made inquiries through some commanders and they answered whenever I asked that one group had left, then another group had left, and later on I found out that there was nobody left at Manjaca. In fact, Herceg Bosna and their representatives were in constant contact with us on this matter and they took over their own people -- I mean, they were constantly in touch with our military authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber has received quite some evidence about what happened in Manjaca. I just think it's fair that the overall impression was not people arrived there and could leave within a couple of days. The overall impression was quite different from that, just for you to know and to give you an opportunity to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I know about Manjaca, but these men did not receive that kind of treatment. Their treatment was completely different because we could find no other place in Banja Luka where such a number of men could be placed. We couldn't find such premises within the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When do you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if I may add --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, when you say these men did not receive that kind of treatment, what do you mean by "that kind of treatment"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean they were not treated as prisoners of war. They were treated as civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean to say that those that were kept in Manjaca were treated as civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I mean, specifically these men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, a couple of brief questions to follow up on that. First, when you distinguish between this group and those that received what you call "that kind of treatment," are you speaking in the latter category of persons who were held at Manjaca in 1992 before it was first closed?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sure. You said: "I know about Manjaca, but these men did not receive that kind of treatment. Their treatment was completely different." You mean their treatment was completely different than other persons who had at some point been held at Manjaca; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I know about Manjaca, what I read in the papers, and I know these men were not treated as prisoners of war. So they had the freedom to go out and move around within certain limits, and they departed, left the area completely after a short while. Now, what the treatment at Manjaca really was, I don't know because when I came there the Manjaca camp had already been closed down. And I protested, I remember, before President Karadzic that Manjaca had been closed, whereas the Serbs were still being held at Zenica. That's all I know, actually. All I know about it is from media reports and certain meetings with the opposite side at negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What you'd read and heard from the opposite side at negotiations was that before it closed the people there were abused and some were killed; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I cannot maintain that with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I -- I heard some witness testimony here --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about whether you personally know whether it happened, and I think that's what you're answering. I'm asking you what you read and what you heard, is it that people there were abused -- people who were detained there were abused, and some were killed, whether or not you have any personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: It's true that happened and I cannot deny any of that. It's a fact that these things have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you remember the first time, roughly, what month, what year, that you read or heard of those allegations?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact month, but it was certainly 1992 at my first meetings with these people. At that time I didn't believe these stories until some evidence began to be led before courts, because I didn't really believe stories. I knew that reports were manipulated, et cetera, but I do believe what the court has established. I cannot say when exactly the first time was that I heard of Manjaca, but I was in Banja Luka beginning with September 1992. I don't know exactly when Mr. Karadzic disbanded that camp, but at that time a large number of Serbs were still held at Zenica, and I protested and others protested very vocally, very strenuously, that Manjaca had been closed down while Serbs were still being held at Zenica because I was aware of what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: With that, sir, I will turn back to early 1992. Now, you mentioned on direct examination that Slobodanka Hrvacanin was the president of the SDS in Zenica. She was also a member of the SDS Main Board; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And among her functions, she would relay information from the SDS at the republic level to you and the other members of the SDS in Zenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Correct, while she was in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You mentioned during direct examination that she left and you became president of the SDS in Zenica. When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: It was the beginning of 1992. I can't remember the date. I didn't become president. I still held the elected post of vice-president, but I actually had the responsibilities of the president. But I was never officially elected president of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I appreciate your precision in explaining that, sir. To achieve a similar precision about your own career, I'm going to ask you about a couple of the dates that you held the positions you mentioned on direct examination. You mentioned that you were an associate of Minister Ostojic. When did you begin working with Minister Ostojic, what month and what year?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I was appointed to the office of Minister Velibor Ostojic in the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: How long did you remain one of his associates?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: As long as Mr. Velibor Ostojic was deputy prime minister, which was some time in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And when did you become president of the agency for the exchange of property?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That was a state agency; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: The government established that agency, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And to whom did you report about the work of that agency?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: There was all sorts of monitoring and vetting by the state security, the police. We wrote reports nonstop, sent them to the government, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you recall which ministry of the government you sent your reports to?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I think it was the ministry of Mr. Brdjanin while he was in power, and after that I sent my reports to the government. Mr. Momir Jugic would come to see me as my contact. He was working on a project of free movement of civilians. He was a representative of the government, and he came to me regularly. So they were informed on a regular basis. In practice you couldn't do anything much with these property swaps because people dealt with it privately. They would find each other, agree on something, and then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You also mentioned you were appointed to the exchange commission. When were you appointed to that commission?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Right after becoming an associate of Minister Ostojic. He and President Karadzic addressed a letter to the commission - that is to say, to Mr. Bokic - suggesting that I should be appointed to help out with these exchanges of civilians and taking care of the accommodation for refugees. That was my main job while I was working for Minister Ostojic. That position still exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: That [Realtime transcript read in error "fact"] fax still exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, there was a central exchange commission as well as regional and municipal commissions; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Were you affiliated with the central commission or one of the regional or municipal commissions?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I had a connection with the central commission through Professor Janko Dokic, who was a member of that commission, and I worked exclusively with him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: In line 21 on page 20, the word should be "fax," like "facsimile," not "fact."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the way the commission worked was that municipal commissions had to submit lists of persons to be exchanged for approval from higher level commissions; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: In my case I was working on the commission concerning civilian persons, and I can show the Court the document including from the Croatian side. I dealt only with civilians. I didn't have to make any lists except for the moment when they were crossing the separation line. Then I would submit a list to the command of the regiment or the corps so that they know that such and such a number of civilians would be crossing the boundary from our side, and from the other side another number of civilians would also be crossing the same line. And then with Professor Dokic, we would agree on a certain exchange. But civilians, in any case, whether the other side had kept their word or not, I always released civilians to go wherever they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you mention the different geographic areas and military units - this is in paragraph 33 of your statement - had their own exchange commissions. Your commission would co-operate with those military commissions; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: We co-operated with the military commission in so far as we had to meet at the separation line. They were always looking for prisoners of war. Of course we co-operated. We couldn't do without co-operation. We had many cases when the opposite side was looking for civilians, and through these commissions I was looking for those people -- looking for people who were willing to leave, et cetera. It's just that I couldn't go myself to see all these people, visit all these people, to tell them, "You know, your family from the other side is looking for you. Do you want to go or not?" I had to do it through them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I think you've gone a little bit beyond the scope of my question, but I understand that your commission did in fact co-operate with the military commissions; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Absolutely. And I needed their co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You also mention that the Red Cross would be involved in the exchanges. This was the Republika Srpska Red Cross; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. The ICRC would be informed as well as the UNHCR. They had exact information as to when, how many people were crossing over to the other side, in order that food and accommodation be provided, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just to repeat my question: This was the Republika Srpska branch of the Red Cross; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: But we had certain co-operation also with the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Republika Srpska Red Cross was recognised by the International Red Cross at that time? Just if you know or not.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And beginning in 1993, the president of the Republika Srpska Red Cross was Ljiljana Karadzic; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That was Radovan Karadzic's wife?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see we're at the time for the break. I'm about to turn to a new topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are. Witness, we would have a break of 20 minutes. We'd like to see you back after the break. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom. For scheduling purposes, we'll not sit tomorrow. We might finish the -- conclude the testimony of this witness today, perhaps even easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I anticipate being done in the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Not this -- the next, the one after this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. And then we have still some time for the next witness that may perhaps not yet be available or is available, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, our next witness is coming tomorrow night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. That's understood. And in view of the developments this week, it's fully understood that the witness is not yet on standby for later this day, and then we'll hear his testimony starting on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could we have 65 ter 1D02455. And this will be the publication in the Official Gazette of a decision appointing members of the exchange commission in May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: While it comes up - and I see we already have the B/C/S - this is during your time as Minister Ostojic's associate; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, 6th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I think in the B/C/S we actually need the -- yeah, and a little bit higher in the right column.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So these are the members of the exchange commission that you collaborated with, the names that we see here; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders 1D02455.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2455 receives number P6718, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning to a different topic --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'm done with this document, now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- and taking you back to before the war in your role in the SDS, sir, did you know Jovan Tintor?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And he was, among other things, a leading member of the SDS in the Sarajevo area; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you spoke to Mr. Tintor on occasion in 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1991, 1992. Whenever we would meet, we talked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has received evidence that Mr. Tintor --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'm referring to P4583.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- in his own words, that he told the RS Assembly: "I went from municipality to municipality and created military formations on order from my president." And that he said: "We created brigade commanders down to platoon commanders. All this was done by the SDS." Now, Mr. Tintor, in 1991, was involved in arming Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I don't have this information. I think that this is Mr. Tintor boasting. I don't believe that he was forming platoons and brigades. Absolutely not. People self-organised, mostly. I think that this is just propaganda. My experience with him was quite different. He likes to boast a lot, but in the end it all comes to nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So your evidence is you don't know whether -- you don't have personal knowledge whether or not Mr. Tintor was involved in arming; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I just have information about his empty words. Really, just empty words. Just talk, empty talk. But actually what happened was quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has received evidence that in a number of municipalities Serbs received arms from the SDS and the JNA, and one of those was Zenica; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: They definitely did not receive weapons from the SDS. That is incorrect. I don't know. Perhaps it's possible that they stole something from the JNA barracks when they went in there. That is possible. I had that kind of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So your information is that Serbs in Zenica went into the JNA barracks and stole things that you believe to include arms?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I had information that individuals and criminals did that and that even that they sold these weapons to Muslims. I can give you two specific names, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the Defence can inquire about that later if they choose, sir, but the Chamber has also received evidence that more than 1.700 Serbs in Zenica have received arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And we've seen the document a number of times but it's P3030.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, that's a report from the 2nd Military District from the JNA. That's more than a couple of criminals; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I don't know. I would need to look at the document. But I think that's quite a high number, 1.700. It's a whole brigade. It's not possible that that many Serbs had weapons in Zenica, but I would like to look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit P3030 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is the cover page. You can see this is a report from the 2nd Military District, from General Kukanjac, dated 20th of March 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And if we could turn to I believe it's page 11 in the English and 16 in the B/C/S, and if we zoom in on point 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You can see there on the left side of the screen: "Zenica, 1.761"; right? For the moment I'm just asking if you see the number.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we scroll up to the top of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the column heading: "Opstina," or "municipality" is the one we find Zenica in, and "Ljudi," or "man" is the one we find the number in; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Then I'd simply put to you that this JNA report is relaying reliable and accurate information about the arming of Serbs in Zenica at the time.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I'm very surprised by this information because I know that they were constantly saying what they would do, how they would manage. Some of the men did enter the barracks, but I'm hearing for the first time now that it was a question of this many weapons. Could you please clarify for me: Do they only mean the municipality of Zenica or the region of Zenica? I'm sorry, yes, I can see Zepa, Vitez, and so on. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And so having seen that, you understand it to be the municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to leave this topic now and turn to your work with Minister Ostojic. You mentioned that you worked on refugee issues. One of Mr. Ostojic --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: One of the minister's responsibilities was that together with Minister Brdjanin he was tasked to prepare a programme for the accommodation of refugees; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the goal of this programme and of Minister Ostojic was to build new demographic politics and establish the ethnical geographical continuity of the Serb population; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say what their intention was. I worked and I was looking for any possible free space where I would be able to accommodate those people who were asking for my help. I don't know what the goals were that you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I did bother both of them about accommodation for the refugees. Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, could the Prosecution have 65 ter 02382. This is the transcript of the 34th Session of the Republika Srpska Assembly. And once it comes up, I'll be asking for the bottom of page 212 in the English and page 230 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: After seeing the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, which we can see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And we can see Minister Ostojic begins speaking in the middle of the page on the B/C/S and towards the bottom of the page in the English, and he says in the fourth line down in the English: "We were aiming to achieve our goal which was ethnical geographical continuity of Serb population while accommodating the refugees. And actually, we were building new demographic politics for the RS."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Then we turn the page. If we could turn to 213 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: "With this aim, we had two tasks. Those are to as soon as possible shelter and accommodate displaced persons and to find them jobs so that the economical consolidation and later on political integration of their lives in the area would move on." Now, do you see that language in the Serbian version?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So, Minister Ostojic's goal, as he presented it to the assembly, did involve the ethnical geographical continuity of the Serb population; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I don't know if that was his goal. I mean, he did speak clearly here, but I cannot really comment on it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, a portion of this assembly session is admitted as Exhibit P2508. This is not included in the admitted portion. I'd propose to speak with the Defence and agree on additional portions. I note the session has been tendered, I believe in its entirety, as an associated exhibit to the testimony of a witness who will come next week. So we'll just meet about additional portions in between, if that's all right with the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is looking forward to any agreement the parties may reach on extending the scope of the exhibit you just mentioned. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could the Prosecution now have 65 ter 02391. And this will be the 39th Session of the Republika Srpska Assembly in March 1994. And we can see that on the first page. So if we could now have page 168 in the English and page 135 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now here we see Minister Ostojic speaking again, and in the middle of the page in English, towards the bottom in the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm looking in the English at the end of the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He says: "We have to deal with this problem first in order to establish the geographic continuity of the Serbian population in RS area." And then below the number 33 in the English, he says: "There are four areas that are extremely sensitive and which should be worked on. The first one" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are we sure that this is still on the right B/C/S page? I think we should move to page --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You're quite right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- 33. Yes. Could you please resume reading. You said you -- you started?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: "There are four areas ..." There, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see. Yes. "There are four areas ..." which is at the top of page 33, apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Cyrillic exceeds mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, "33" is the same in both languages, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's true, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can follow what Mr. Traldi reads on the top of page 33, Witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So he's mentioned this problem that has to be dealt with in order to establish geographic continuity. And now he says: "There are four areas that are extremely sensitive and which should be worked on. The first one is old Herzegovina, in the area of Srbinje, Visegrad, Rogatica." Now, Srbinje is what had previously been called Foca; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And that area is on the Drina River; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So the second one is Birac in the area of Vlasenica, Bratunac, Zvornik. That area, too, is on the Drina; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The third one is Posavina in two directions, along the Sava river and outskirts of Trebava, Vlasic, et cetera. The fourth one is Sana Una area, and the fifth is Vrbas area. And he explains for a couple of lines where those fall, and then says: "We lack the population ..." Do you see that text?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, what he's identifying here were areas where efforts were being made to resettle Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: It's what it states here. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And based on your experience as his associate, that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: My experience is completely different. I don't know what Mr. Ostojic meant by this, but I am one of those people - and I can prove that to this Tribunal - that at the beginning of the war in 1991 publicly said over the media that we need to be careful not to destroy anything, because at the end of everything we will all come back to where we come from. I tried to speak with Mr. Ostojic a few times. He would say, "Take people here or there," but it's very difficult for anybody to implement anything like this. And he's dead, so it's not very nice to say anything like this about him, but it was impossible to direct people in that way. People would go to a different area or abroad or something. I could never guide people to these areas that he refers to here. In any case, it was impossible. That was already engulfed by war. There was destruction there. So you would need to have a lot of funds to be able to implement something like this. It wasn't really possible. I was among those who believed - and I can prove that - that everybody would return to where they originally came from. What they wanted was of a temporary nature. So I can't comment on that. I was aware that what was being done was a temporary measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So, sir, you've answered several questions, but I'd like to return to the one I asked, which is: It's true, isn't it, that this is an area where efforts were being made to resettle Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: What do you mean, "efforts made"? Because it was not possible to accommodate people there. It was not possible. It was not possible. It was destroyed. I knew the area. I toured the area and I knew the situation very well. It wasn't possible to do this without enormous investments. I mean, I wouldn't even mention it. They could say whatever they wanted at the government, but what was actually the situation on the ground was completely different. You had to see for yourself, know what was going on. The easiest thing is to talk sitting in your office. I think you would agree with me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Let's turn to your own work, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this, too, I believe has been tendered in its entirety as an associated exhibit to the evidence of a witness scheduled to testify next week, and I'd just propose that we deal with it at that time and I'll speak with the Defence in the interim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic agrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So turning to your work at the agency for exchange of property, you assisted a number of Muslims in leaving Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Assisted? I don't know whether that was assisting, but when people wanted to leave, they would report to us and then they would leave. And the same thing applied to the Serbs who were coming from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll just ask a couple of questions about your procedures. They had to pay a fee to leave; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: That depended on where they were going, in which direction. They had to pay for the bus and so on. Yes, yes. Sometimes there was a taxi. Yes -- I mean, yes, it was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Those fees for bus fare would be a hundred or more deutschmarks; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And sometimes even more. Sometimes several hundred or more than a thousand?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: It depended. It depended on -- I mean, it's not correct if they were going to these areas. Only if they were going to Hungary they had to pay quite high tax there, because I think they were giving to the Hungarians either 4- or 500 German marks and then the passport. So they would pay the Hungarians about a thousand marks. If they were going somewhere within Bosnia-Herzegovina it was a hundred or 150, depending on the driver, how much he asked for and how much he had to pay for the trucks and the other transport. But that was about how much it ranged. When you mentioned 1.000 marks, 600 of that went to the Hungarians, for them to be able to enter Hungary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And in many cases they also had to sign forms requesting permission to leave; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Permission to leave? They didn't ask for permission to leave. I don't know how it was by municipality by municipality. Did they have to cancel their telephone, electricity. They didn't ask for permission. All I did was make lists and submit them to the authorised command that on such and such a day we would be crossing the border. That was the gist. I don't know if that was a permission or what it was, but that's how it went.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I won't insist on the word "permission" for the moment, sir, but I take it you would agree that they would sign forms requesting to leave; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: A request? A request is when they asked to leave. However, all I needed was the form that they filled in, general particulars, so that I would be able to announce to the command. That's what the form was used for. Nobody could forbid a civilian from going somewhere, whether they could go or not. They had the right to go wherever they wanted. That was the main thing. The form contained their general particulars that I would record, then a list would be drafted which I submitted to the command, and then we would come to the line of separation. The list would be checked. When they were going across the border to Hungary, the form was also filled in and it was checked. There was no permission. Civilians were allowed to go without any problems. I would like you to point to me a single case when somebody was not permitted to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Without looking at individual cases at the moment, sir, the forms had to be given to the military command so that people could cross the line of separation, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Of course. All border crossings were controlled. That is logical -- sorry, not the border but the line of separation. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to turn to the exchange commission now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And could we have 65 ter 11889 brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, we see here a document on the exchange of prisoners from the central commission for the exchange of prisoners and civilians, and it bears the stamp of the SRK, intelligence and security affairs organ. Now, this says, among the addressees, that it's being sent to the president of the RS Assembly, the security organ of the SRK, and the Novo Sarajevo CSB; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So the exchange commission is informing political, military, and police institutions about the exchange it's conducting; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: That is so here, but I'm really unable to comment on this document. When I worked, I did not work in this way. All I asked was security from the security services centre in Banja Luka. So I would ask for an escort of two vehicles, I would announce when I would be going, and I would ask for an escort by the military police so that nothing would happen to us on the road. And that is why I would notify them about when we were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: As for this thing, this is a matter for the political structure, so I never had anything to do with that. This is the first time that I'm seeing this type of notification. What does that mean, that the president of the assembly is being informed about this? I don't know what the intention was when everybody was being informed. All I -- the only ones that I submitted notification to would be the command and the time of the departure. That was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, would you please focus your answer on the question. The question was just whether this was addressed to the persons Mr. Traldi referred to. He didn't ask you whether this is how you did it or how someone else did it. Could you please focus your answer on the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one objection: I think that this document should not be tendered through this witness because he does not have any knowledge about this document and is unable to assist in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I think it was common practice developed over the last period of time that if a witness testifies about a certain matter and if a document sheds light on the same issue - and here, for example, the witness says that this is not how he did it - then that becomes relevant in this context. And therefore whether we call it introduced through the witness or in relation to the witness's testimony, but it's not a reason not to admit. Mr. Traldi, I just set out the general -- not guidance but the practice in this Chamber. Would you like to add something before I give a ruling?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just very briefly to say that I'd understood the witness's answer to confirm that he, too, would communicate with the police and the military but not with the political branch, and that was the only distinction between what we saw in the document and his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 11889 receives number P6719, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir, discussing exchanges. In paragraph 29 of your statement, you say: "There was no parity in the exchange..." And the Bosnian Serb side sought to exchange groups on an all-for-all basis; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the transcript, I think, through my own fault, recorded me a little bit imprecisely. Let me ask the question again if I might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's now corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Then I'll leave it as it stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So, Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic is not supposed to speak aloud. Mr. Lukic, if Mr. Mladic wants to consult you, he can do it at an inaudible volume. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Would it assist if I repeated the most pertinent part of the question, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: You can repeat it. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb side sought to exchange groups on an all-for-all basis; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So I just want to look at one example of a document setting out that policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can 65 ter 19958 be brought to our screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it 199 or 119?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- and I apologise, my speed may have been off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's more likely to have been my mistake, Your Honour. So I see we have it now. My notes may be in error as to this document, so I'll come back after the break if I have any time remaining. And now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on page 3 of your list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of exhibits to be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I see it is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But I've reversed the number of this one and another in my outline, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can 65 ter 31166 please be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is going to deal with one of the exchanges that you participated in. This is a document coming from the Mrkonjic Grad department of the Banja Luka CRDB. And it notes that the military and civilian commissions of Republika Srpska and the so-called BH Republic met on 27 July 1994 in Ljubin Han on the line of demarcation between the VRS and the so-called BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, in order to avoid further confusion 65 ter 3116?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 6, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not clear on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Looking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Again, it's 31116 in its totality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: All right. Not to further any confusion, but I believe it's 31166.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I apologise. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As do I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last number is definitive. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So beginning with the document again, this is a document coming from the Mrkonjic Grad department of the Banja Luka CRDB, and it notes in the first paragraph that: "The military and civilian commissions of Republika Srpska and the so-called BH Republic met on 27 July 1994 in Ljubin Han; i.e., on the line of demarcation between the VRS and the so-called BH army (halfway between Borike and Turbe)." And it notes -- I'll just summarize the next couple of paragraphs for efficiency. It notes that the BH army brought eight VRS POWs, it notes that the VRS brought ten BH army soldiers, and the civilian commissions brought along four buses full of civilians, it says between 170 and 217, most of whom were elderly people and women and children. Do you see that language?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And looking at paragraph 6, it says that when you headed to the scene, so this is an exchange that you participated in; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So what we're seeing here is, I'd put to you, an exchange which primarily consists of civilians leaving RS territory; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'd tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31166 receives number P6720, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And can 65 ter 19602 be brought to the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And as this is brought up, I'd put to you that the Republika Srpska exchange commissions would exchange non-Serb civilians for captured VRS soldiers at times. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I am not aware that these things happened, because I never had such cases where civilians would be exchanged for soldiers. I don't know what was done in Goradze. I see the document but I really did not have such a case myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But, Witness, the previous document where you are mentioned to have participated mentioned civilians being brought in a bus, four buses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the civilians were brought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- did participate in an exchange of civilians on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were not exchanged. They were released to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I expected the Prosecutor to ask me about that document, and I'm sorry that -- I know what was done. It doesn't have to be written here. They were released to go free.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's reported, not to linger on the previous document, but the Mrkonjic Grad department of the CRDB was reporting that that was part of the exchange; right? If it would be useful, we can call it back up.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I think it would help, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have P6720, again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this was done, looking at the document, these civilians were brought and taken across the confrontation lines in the context of a meeting between the military and civilian exchange commissions of Republika Srpska and the exchange commission of the BH Republic; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Correct. May I further clarify this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: This event remained etched in my mind. What I see here about the elderly woman is not true, because while the military commissions were negotiating, I allowed our buses to cross over the line. And I made a huge mistake. I let them cross over with civilians to the other side, and suddenly the buses stopped coming back. I didn't know that military policemen had approached, took out a very young man, a civilian, a man younger than myself - and I was then 40-something; that man was far younger - and he was an officer of the former JNA. I had put him on that bus because he had come with his family and signed up, but one of those military policemen either knew him from before or recognised him. They took the man out. They wanted him to produce some additional permits in order to let him go. I went back, made a phone call, and the whole thing was settled very quickly. He was put back on the bus together with his wife and children. This, I am emphatically maintaining, is not connected with an exchange of civilians. I was supposed to receive some civilians from Bugojno, Travnik, et cetera. The opposite side did not comply with our agreement. I learnt my lesson and I never did the same thing again. So it's not true that an elderly person was concerned. It was a very young man, an officer of the JNA. They left without any problem and I got my buses back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's Azem Omerbasic as mentioned in the last paragraph?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember the name after so much time. But we can check. He was a JNA officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, I want to direct your --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Just a moment. Could we look at the next part of the B/C/S version so the witness can follow your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Of course. If we could -- I think we could just scroll down. No, up the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I'm very happy we can see this because I know I've been telling the truth to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we go back to the first page in the B/C/S. I want to look at the third and fourth paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The third paragraph reads: "Our civilian commission brought almost four buses full of civilians (the exact number has not been ascertained, although there were between 170 and 217), most of whom were elderly people and women with children." In the fourth paragraph the document continues: "The exchange began at 1315 hours, when the first bus headed to the place where the commissions were working ..." So I'd put to you that the Mrkonjic Grad department of the CRDB is reporting here that the exchange began when the first bus of civilians headed to the place where the commissions were working; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: The first, second, bus, when it happened, really no. But these arbitrary figures, four buses of 170 to 218, tells us how frivolous this is. There was no elderly woman. They were all much younger than myself. I did bring four buses. I do not dispute that. But there were all sorts of people of all age groups, even younger people. Not only women and children. This was done very unprofessionally and very sloppily. I really have --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I put it again --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I mean, 100 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think again you're answering a different question than what I've asked. What I'm putting to you is simply that the Mrkonjic Grad CRDB is reporting that the exchange began with the departure of the first bus of civilians. That's the literal text of the report; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And so I'd put to you that they are, in fact, treating those civilians as part of the exchange. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: No, no. It was not like part of the exchange. I normally let these people move from one bus to another and they moved their things, too. And the military commissions were exchanging prisoners of war. I was expecting to receive the civilians that were due to me and they hadn't brought anyone, but I still let the civilians that I was keeping, because I -- I let them go because I was told that I must not bring anyone back. These people were those who had requested to leave. They had visas for third countries, some of them. They had expressly wanted to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note it's close to time for the break. I'm done with this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have one question for the witness. You said: "I was expecting to receive the civilians that were due to me ..." Why were they due to you if everyone was free to leave? Yes, please explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, they were due to me. I meant to say that I was claiming those civilians and I had an agreement with them that these civilians would be brought to me, to Ljubin Han, because this Sefer who is mentioned here is a man to whom I talked on the radio twice a week. We exchanged information about whether people on my side or his side wanted to cross over. We swapped information about that and talked at least twice a week by radio. Those were the people that I was claiming. Sefer even had told me that he had some people who wanted to cross over to Republika Srpska. We had that kind of communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 10 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just to use the time efficiently and having corrected my notes or had them corrected, I wonder if, as the witness is being brought in, we might already pull up 65 ter 19558.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document 19588 -- is it 588 or 558?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
