utterances.text: Now, if you recall, sir, last session we discussed the Bosnian Serbs advocacy of all-for-all exchanges, and in the second paragraph here, and this is a document bearing General Tolimir's name and dated the 4th of June, 1995, we read him say: "We believe it is necessary to insist on observing the 'all-for-all' principle so that the exchange is carried out in one day in arranged locations." Now, I would just stop there and ask you: It's correct, isn't it, that your evidence is that's the principle that the Bosnian Serbs advocated, this all-for-all exchange; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean, my principle. This concerns prisoners of war. Civilians are an entirely different issue. They were not sent for an exchange. They were just released to go free. That was our principle, to allow everybody freedom of movement. All civilians, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But, sir, if I could --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- interrupt for a moment, and we'll get to that. We'll get to the civilians and prisoners of war. But if I look at your evidence on temporary transcript page 39, I asked you at lines 18 and 19: "The Bosnian Serb side sought to exchange groups on an all-for all-basis; right?" And you said: "Yes, that's right." That was your evidence at that time; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And so what General Tolimir is advocating here is consistent with the Bosnian Serbs position as you described it a few transcript pages ago; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: If we're talking about POWs, I know that it was all-for-all, but exchanges of civilians did not go along those lines. They were allowed to go wherever they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 19558 receives number P6721, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, if we could have Exhibit P4008.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is a document, an order, as it's identified, also coming from General Tolimir. And the first paragraph refers to an agreement reached on the 1st of October 1994. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And it refers to the exchange of a prisoner -- of prisoners held in Gorazde and Konjic and Sarajevo in the first paragraph, and then in the second to the exchange of prisoners -- Muslim prisoners being held in Foca, Rudo, Visegrad, and some in Batkovic and Butmir. Do you see that as well?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Where it refers to Butmir, that's another name used to refer to Kula prison; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I really don't know. I know about the Kula prison, but Butmir? I was convinced that it was a prison on the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, looking at the long paragraph in the English that begins: "The Sarajevo Romanija Corps ..." I'm going to call your attention to the end of that paragraph. There General Tolimir writes: "It should be kept in mind that in the exchanges we received captured soldiers of the Republika Srpska while we mostly give them civilians." So what General Tolimir is saying here is that the Republika Srpska authorities were exchanging civilians, receiving back captured soldiers; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I would not agree with you because that's not the way we did things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Whether it happened somewhere --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, that wasn't the question. The question was not whether it happened. The question was whether you agree that that is what General Tolimir is saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. Then I didn't understand the question. Yes, it is stated so here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you claim in paragraph 30 of your statement that the army didn't deal with the departure and exchange of civilians. That's exactly what General Tolimir is referring to here; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I continue to maintain that the military was not there, where I was moving. But what General Tolimir says, it's probably true because we never stopped a military conscript from crossing over to the other side as a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd ask that we call up 65 ter 19602.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And this is going to be a prisoner exchange report from the Bosnian State Commission for Exchange dated 5th October 1994, about 12 days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 2, and in the English it will be the second paragraph. In the B/C/S we are actually towards the bottom of the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this paragraph starts: "The aggressor ..." and that was language that the Bosnians commonly used to refer to the Bosnian Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: "The aggressor took advantage of the exchange to expel 87 Bosniaks, Muslims, from ..." and then it lists a number of villages. Those are villages in eastern Bosnia, including in Rogatica; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I don't know, but I don't see that Rogatica is mentioned. Knezina, Kramerci, Kolina. I don't know where you see Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I wasn't suggesting that it was mentioned. What I was suggesting was that one or more of those are in Rogatica municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I could not confirm that because I really don't know these places. I passed through Rogatica quite by chance a few times, but I don't know these places.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 3 in the English, and we'll be turning I believe to page 3 in the B/C/S as well, under the word "Analysis."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So at the beginning of the analysis it gives a number of dates, and then says: "We managed to implement most of the 1 October 1994 agreement relating to prisoner exchange." Now, that's the same date for an agreement referred to in General Tolimir's order that we just saw, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And it says: "Karadzic's Bosnian Serbs freed a total of 247 prisoners from various prisons in Foca, Rudo, Visegrad, Rogatica, Batkovic, as well as Lukavica and Kula ..." A number of those are the prisons that were listed in General Tolimir's order; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Then it refers to the legal authorities of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina freeing 135 members and associates of the enemy army and other categories of citizens detained on reasonable grounds of suspicion that they had committed conflict-related crimes. And it goes into the structure of the freed persons. And it says: "Karadzic's Serbs freed a total of 19 members of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina armed forces, only three of whom were captured in combat." And it breaks it down. It says: "20 of the freed persons were women, 3 were children under the age of 10." And below that it says: "Four of the freed prisoners are older than 70. One is older than 84 and one older than 86." Do you see that language?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And so what I put to you is that this document reflects just what General Tolimir said, that in the exchange the Bosnian Serbs were receiving captured soldiers and were mostly giving civilians. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Again, I say this is what it states in the document, but I'm absolutely unaware of this. So if you're asking me is this what the document says, it does. As for whether this is correct or not, I cannot say because this was happening in a completely different part of the Bosnia-Herzegovina. Again, I state before this Tribunal that this is not how I did things. I did not exchange civilians for prisoners. If the civilians came, that was all very well. If they wanted to leave, I would let them go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 19602 receives number P6722, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can 65 ter 19313 be brought to our screens?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is the last document I'll show you today. It will be dated 5 April 1995 and reflect minutes from a session of the Bosnian Serb Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that we turn, now that we've seen the cover page, to page 69 of the English and 62 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And General Tolimir is speaking. And in the middle of the paragraph that begins: "Never mind that he is miscalculating ..." looking at the third line, he says: "If Mr. Glogovac is a socially-owned agency, then approval can be requested, approval given for emigration in accordance with the Geneva Convention that has been nicely proposed in our memorandum, according to the Geneva Convention on War. It was written privately for civilians --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Show down. Slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I'll pick up at the word "civilians."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: "Every civilian has the right to choose his place of residence and to go where he is safer, and we could draw up a form which this Glogovac will give Muslims to fill in. It is precisely spelled out in the Geneva Conventions that they wish to move out while war conflicts are going on, and he voluntarily wishes to move out to the territory of a third country because he does not want to take part in the war conflicts. So the moment that he signs that he is leaving he has expressed and documented his will. I did that while I was in Knin and not a single Croat ever returned, and we showed the papers to the UN and that is why the Croats cannot bring them back even by force." So what I'm going to put to you is that General Tolimir is describing forms that are, in fact, the forms you described in the previous session that Muslims would fill in when they were leaving the RS and going to third countries or going to Bosnian-held territory. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I can see what is written here and it is clear to me. However, I categorically state that I never received any papers or forms from anyone, including General Tolimir. I don't know what they were thinking when they were doing this. Perhaps it's related to the agreement of the late Professor Koljevic and the representative of the International Red Cross, Mr. Sam Ruga, who signed an agreement about civilians, and that they could do what is said here. But I categorically state before this Court that I never received any forms to this effect, so I really don't know what they talked about, what they meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just to conclude, I'd put to you you've confirmed you gave departing Muslim civilians forms, you've confirmed that they filled them out, you've confirmed that those documented they voluntarily wished to leave. That's all true, isn't it? A simple "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: No. Categorically no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The witness's previous testimony on this matter speaks for itself and so I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Given the length of the document, I'd ask that it be marked for identification for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 19313 receives number P6723, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6723 is marked for identification. Mr. Stojanovic, any questions in redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few, Your Honours. Perhaps it would be good to stay with this document for a moment while we still have it in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Glogovac, perhaps it would be good if you told the Trial Chamber according to your best recollection how this process went in which you, as part of the agency, took part the process of the population wishing to leave the territory of your area of their own free will.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I already -- I can say before this Tribunal that at one point prosecutors came to Banja Luka. They wanted to discuss this topic, something that had to do with these forms. I said that I could be a potential witness for Krajisnik and Karadzic, and they did not force me to discuss this because I said that I needed to remain objective. The process - this is the way it went from the Muslim and Croat side - they asked me to bring certain families that had remained behind because their families were looking for them. They would come to us. It was just a plain form with your first name, last name, date of birth, address, and the person would state where they wanted to go. There was nothing else on the form, whether they wanted to come back or not, what would happen to their property, nothing like that. I'm sorry, I am going quite fast again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what did you use this form for in the continued process of the transfer of those people?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: The form was used to make a list to report to the responsible command where and when we would be crossing into the territory. So that was the only purpose of that form. It could not be used for anything else, for any other purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any situations when the citizens would voice their desire to leave the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and where they wanted to go to western Europe, for example?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, there were numerous such cases. Mostly people wanted to go to a different country. Some of them even had visas. And often they would be quite persistent until we made it possible for them to leave through Croatia or Hungary or another different area of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at document 65 ter 31168 in e-court, please. 31168.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Glogovac, this is a document where your name is mentioned. I would like you to read it, and then I would like to ask you this: The process of seeking permission for unhindered passage, is this document a response to such a request made by you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Let me first read this aloud.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, you don't have to read it out loud. Read it for yourself and then answer.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. We would announce to the military organs and to the police, and then the police would provide two or three vehicles as security because I didn't want to allow anything unfortunate to happen on the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And if people were prepared to go to Bosnia and Herzegovina that was under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the line of separation, the front line had to be crossed. Whose permission would you ask for then?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I would then ask the corps command to allow us to pass freely, and I would also ask for security to provide -- to be provided by the civilian police, and I would also ask for a vehicle from the military police just in case any of the soldiers were making any problems. When crossing I would always have both police and military escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you answered Judge Orie's question about "the persons that were due to me, that I was expecting," who were you specifically thinking of? Where were they supposed to be coming from?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Well, if I remember correctly, these would be ethnic Serbs who were living in the area of the then-Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was Travnik, Novi Travnik, Bugojno, a part of Zenica. That was the area that I meant. And so if anybody wanted to come, Sefer Samir would usually report to me how many such persons wished to cross to our side. So I do have requests from the commission asking that these people cross to the territory of Republika Srpska. I received them from Mr. Sefer. These documents can always be presented to the Court. They are still available.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look again at P6720.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a document you had an opportunity to see when you were cross-examined by the Prosecutor, and you also answered a question from Judge Moloto on this document. Could you please focus on paragraph 2 of this document. Can this paragraph refresh your memory to the effect that it was precisely when you brought those civilians in four buses, simultaneously there was an exchange of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: That's right. It happened not only here. There were more cases of that. We can look at the exchange of prisoners between Herceg Bosna and our side, on which occasion I accepted or received 201 civilians. It happened both with the Croat side and the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I will conclude. At any time while doing the job you described, did you gain the impression or perhaps have specific knowledge that there were open and deliberate takeovers of civilians who were made to leave the area where they were living by force?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: No. During my tenure, no. Sometimes, I can tell the Court, they would even sleep over at my own apartment before departure. I would never allow anything of the sort, nor did anyone ever complain that it happened. There were cases when people didn't want to go. In response to a query from the family on the other side, they would write a letter sending their greetings and saying they want to stay where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the main reason why these people were departing?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you about my own case. I fled. I left. Terrible things happened in our area. We have terrible experiences from World War I and World War II. Many times I made an appeal through TV Zenica: "Please, do not all run away." However, the fear was overwhelming, and there was also propaganda. There were combat operations in April 1992. A large group of refugees came from Derventa, and I couldn't imagine what had happened to those people. The media went wild. I went to see these people together with a neighbour of mine to ask these people what they had fled from, what the Serbs had done to them. They just said, "Serbs are surrounding Derventa. We are afraid of revenge. We just fear for our lives. We wanted to leave."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much for the answers you provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us about people who were going to Hungary. Were they transported in buses or trucks or ...?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Up to the Hungarian border, they went by bus. From there on, I don't know. We had various reports. But up to the Hungarian border --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They travelled by bus. How many people would a bus take on average?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Well, as many as there were seats. There were smaller and larger buses. It depended on how many people had signed up. But they were not overcrowded. We always tried to leave some space free until the last moment in case somebody appeared at the last -- at the eleventh hour. It was a long way to travel, so we didn't want them to be overcrowded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How do I have to understand this, there to be then 40 people on the bus approximately? Or would there be 5 people on the bus or 70?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there were buses that had 35 to 40 seats. There were buses of 50-plus seats, up to 70. There were all sorts of buses. But there were enough seats. I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now to whom did those who were transferred have to pay?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Part of the fee they paid to the agency for the bus and the passports, and part of the money they had to keep because they had to pay it to the Hungarians at the border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you mean the agency -- were you involved in the agency?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you said that, in response to a question put to you by Mr. Traldi, when you mentioned 1.000 deutschmarks, 600 of that went to the Hungarians. Do I understand that then 400 remained with the agency?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: No. Part was needed to arrange passports because they didn't have passports, and the rest was to cover the cost of the buses because at that time the buses were very expensive because petrol was very expensive. So it was a costly affair to get a bus. There were also cases when people didn't have any money, and I have certificates for this, that we provided money to people who were indigent because they had been literally kicked out of their houses or -- well, because of other circumstances, they didn't have any money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there written documentation about these financial arrangements for those who left?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN GLOGOVAC
utterances.text: I had them. I believe they still exist. But we had rigorous controls, and I believe every day somebody checked exactly which monies were paid into which account and how much. But we don't have any documentation of the money that was paid to the Hungarians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking this, and I'm also addressing the Defence, because until now we've seen that the testimony of the witness sometimes differs from what we see in documentation. I do not know what the basis of Mr. Traldi's questions were about the money being paid, 100, 150 deutschmarks. But of course the Chamber would very -- be very much assisted in assessing the weight to be given to the testimony by any underlying documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we will certainly endeavour to find this, but I would like to clarify one thing. Witness, this is documentation you provided to the Brdjanin Defence or is it still in the archive of the agency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was provided to the Brdjanin Defence team and that's why the OTP requested the same documents later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, if you have any documentation about it. Of course, we are trying to -- to find as much -- well, not to find, but to seek that as much evidence are presented to the Chamber as possible so as to enable us to assess the probative value of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We'll consult our archives, Mr. President. I can say that my basis was not official records but a number of statements from persons who'd been transported out, and explained that they had paid to leave under those circumstances. So I haven't seen the exact documents that you're looking for, but we're happy to check our records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the parties would do so. Have the questions in redirect triggered any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Witness, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, questions put to you by the parties, questions put to you by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm reminded to inquire, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we need the witness for --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's first allow the witness to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm reminded to inquire if Mr. Stojanovic intended to tender 65 ter 31168 which he used on redirect, and if he does we would have no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Let me just tender for the record the document 65 ter 31168.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31168 receives number D621, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D621 is admitted into evidence. Since there are no witnesses at this moment to be examined, we adjourn for the day but also for the week, and we will resume on Monday, 9.30 in the morning - that is, Monday the 8th of September, if I'm not mistaken. Ms. Bibles, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could take five minutes to follow up on a question from the Trial Chamber about one of the exhibits from Witness Adzic's testimony, or I could do that later. I'm in the Court's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we have some spare time at this moment, so perhaps we do it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, Exhibit 3951 was used with Witness Adzic last week. At transcript 24804, the Chamber noted that the document refers to a Stevo, S-t-e-v-o, Drljaca, and asked the Prosecution to explain why we believe that this refers to Simo, S-i-m-o, Drljaca. P3951 refers to a massacre committed by the Prijedor police under a "Stevo Drljaca." The correct name of the Prijedor police chief is Simo Drljaca as noted by RM16 at transcript 17368 in relationship to this specific document. Drljaca is additionally identified as the chief of the Prijedor police in the trial record at T17838, T2589 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the first transcript reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes. 2589 -- oh, I'm sorry, the one before that was 17838 and transcript reference 17926. There are additionally a large number of exhibits which have been admitted which also identify the chief of the Prijedor police as Simo Drljaca. For the responsibility of the Prijedor police under Chief Drljaca for the massacre, we refer Your Honours to the evidence of RM60, RM96, and RM97. We have also searched our demographic records for any reference to a Stevo Drljaca who might fit this description in this time-period, and we have found no such individuals. It is the Prosecution's position that 3951 report -- the report reflects a mistake in the first name, that "Stevo" should be "Simo." Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bibles. Any comments by the Defence in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I couldn't find in this document the name, so I don't know the context; although, my learned friend told us the context. And I can confirm that in 1992 the head of Prijedor police was Simo Drljaca. So it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it seems --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- there is no dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- there may not be any dispute about that. But then 3951, Ms. Bibles, could you remind me where we find Stevo, in what context, so that we --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I believe it was page 4 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look. Perhaps we could have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'm operating from memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can't find it immediately on that page, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can it be brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: It should -- at the top of the English section of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let me see.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And the previous page in the English version describes the massacre. Oh, I'm sorry, Your Honour, it is actually in this paragraph that describes the massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is obvious from the document that it is Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there is no dispute that the reference to Stevo Drljaca should be understood as a reference to Simo Drljaca. May I take it because there is only one such massacre known where 150 people died on the same route --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And only one head of Prijedor CSB at that time by the name of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- Simo Drljaca. And also in connection with the Koricanske Stijene massacre in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the parties agree that this reference is about the Koricanske Stijene massacre and that the reference to Drljaca is -- should be read as "Simo Drljaca." Thank you, Ms. Bibles. Thank you, Mr. Lukic. We then now really adjourn for the day and for the week and will resume Monday, the 8th of September, 9.30 in the morning. I do not know yet whether it will be Courtroom II or whether Courtroom I will be fixed by then. It will be Courtroom I, Madam Registrar indicates to me. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 8th day of September, 2014, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.02 p.m.,
